title: Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 117) SR&ED Ruling
subject: TCC appeal assessing SR&ED eligibility for iterative food-product formulation and manufacturing process development.
summary: Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108, occasionally referenced as 2023 TCC 117) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling relevant to Canadian manufacturers. Chief Justice Rossiter allowed Canafric's 2013–2016 appeals, holding that analyzing why failed recipes missed requirements is systematic investigation, not trial and error, and that rejected hypotheses are technological advancement.
metaDescription: Learn about the Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 117) decision in the Tax Court of Canada regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Citation Clarification

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) in Canafric Inc. v. The King represents a watershed ruling in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence, particularly for corporate taxpayers operating in traditional manufacturing, commercial food processing, and formulation-based industries. From a formal procedural standpoint, Canadian tax practitioners must note a recurring citation discrepancy in secondary legal indices: while occasionally referenced in query databases under the neutral citation 2023 TCC 117 (which officially corresponds to the solicitor-client privilege and subsection 103(1) partnership reallocation decision in 632738 Alberta Ltd. v. The King, rendered on August 10, 2023), the official neutral citation for the Canafric SR&ED judgment handed down by Chief Justice Eugene P. Rossiter on July 26, 2023, is Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108. The appeal consolidated four General Procedure dockets—2018-677(IT)G, 2019-3835(IT)G, 2020-1571(IT)G, and 2020-1574(IT)G—encompassing the Appellant's 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016 taxation years.
The Taxpayer's Claim and the Minister's Challenge

The Appellant, Canafric Inc. ("Canafric"), operates a food manufacturing business specialized in developing frozen pies mainly for the Canadian and United States markets, for customers including Costco, Loblaw's, Metro, Mortimer's, National Foods, Swiss Chalet & Cara Foods, Alimentation Couche-Tard, and Longo's. Throughout the 2013 to 2016 taxation years, Canafric carried on a series of food-science and process-engineering projects aimed at developing new frozen pie formulations or achieving incremental improvements to pre-existing frozen products. In developing these products, Canafric had to balance "health" requirements (reducing salt and fat contents) against "taste" requirements (maintaining good taste), together with project-specific customer targets such as shelf life without artificial preservatives, texture, and product integrity through the freeze/thaw process.

Canafric claimed current SR&ED expenditures pursuant to section 37 of the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act") and corresponding Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) pursuant to section 127 of the Act. Following technical and financial audits conducted by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)—which included an on-site facility review on September 14, 2015, at Canafric's new facility (not the Burlington plant where the 2013 activities took place), involving CRA representatives David Zhou (Research and Technology Advisor), George Papadopoulos (Financial Reviewer), and Azza Hassanein (Research and Technology Manager) regarding the 2013 claim, as well as a subsequent on-site meeting on March 8, 2018, originally meant to review two projects (1501 and 1502) in the 2015 and 2016 claims, during which the CRA's advisor chose to focus on project 1501—the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") disallowed seven multi-year SR&ED projects. Excluding the undisclosed quantum for the three disallowed projects in the 2014 taxation year, the Minister denied $343,449 in deductible SR&ED expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across the 2013, 2015, and 2016 taxation years. The financial and project breakdown across the four taxation years is summarized in the table below.

The CRA disallowed the claims on the basis that Canafric's formulation and testing activities did not constitute "experimental development" within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Act. Specifically, the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor, David Zhou, took the position that reducing fat and salt contents was not a technical challenge because such techniques are transferable from one product to another (accepting, for project 1501, a technological uncertainty only for the first of its twelve products, and rejecting project 1602 on the basis that "a pie is a pie"); for projects 1304 and 1306 he acknowledged a technological uncertainty but considered the supporting documentation insufficient, and the 2014 claim was rejected without technical review under section 5.11.0 of the CRA's Claim Review Manual after a conference call scheduled for September 9, 2016 did not take place. The CRA further took the position that Canafric relied on a "trial and error" approach, trying various recipes to reach its targets without attempting to explain or analyze why each recipe did not work, and CRA witnesses testified that oral or "anecdotal" information, such as that provided by Canafric's Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Suvrut Pandya, is not sufficient in itself without independent objective evidence.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The Canadian statutory regime governing R&D tax incentives traces its legislative origin to 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act, which first permitted Canadian corporations to deduct research and development outlays against revenue. Under the modern Income Tax Act, paragraphs 18(1)(a) and 18(1)(b) generally prohibit the deduction of outlays not incurred for the purpose of gaining or producing income from a business and disallow capital expenditures. Section 37(1) of the Act provides a targeted statutory exception, permitting taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature (capital expenditures having ceased to qualify for SR&ED after 2013) incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada via an accumulating SR&ED expenditure pool, while subsections 127(5) and 127(9) (alongside section 127.1 for refundable CCPC credits) entitle claimants to ITCs calculated as a percentage of qualified SR&ED expenditures.

The statutory gateway to both section 37 expenditure deductions and section 127 ITCs is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED through a two-pronged structure: the "How" requirement, which mandates a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," and the "Why" requirement, which mandates that the work be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge—comprising basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a) or applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b)—or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement under paragraph 248(1)(c) (experimental development). Paragraph 248(1)(c) specifically encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Paragraph 248(1)(d) extends eligibility to work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, but only to the extent that such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Conversely, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) explicitly exclude market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

To operationalize subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the canonical five-factor judicial test formulated by Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), and subsequently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA) (at p. 5089), CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (affirming CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)), and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (at para. 12). Under this binding framework, the taxpayer bears the burden of establishing on a balance of probabilities that five cumulative criteria are satisfied: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.
The Tax Court of Canada's Final Holding

Chief Justice Rossiter allowed Canafric's appeals in their entirety across all four taxation years (2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016) and gave the parties 60 days to file written submissions on entitlement to and quantum of costs; a tax-related award of $37,250 under docket 2018-677(IT)G was subsequently paid to Makki Law in trust for Canafric Inc., as reported in the Public Accounts of Canada 2025. At paragraphs 115 and 116 of the Reasons for Judgment, Chief Justice Rossiter held that the Appellant had "successfully established that the 2013, 2015, 2015 and 2016 SR&ED Claims met all five criteria" (the repeated "2015" being an evident typographical slip in the Reasons, as the judgment covers the 2013 to 2016 taxation years) of Northwest Hydraulic and concluded unconditionally: "I am more than satisfied the Appellant discharged its burden."

The Court found that Mr. Suvrut Pandya, who served as Canafric's CEO, oversaw the development work without conducting it himself, and was involved at every stage of the CRA review process across all four taxation years, was a credible, reliable and "very impressive" witness whose factual testimony, together with the documentation Canafric provided, supported the claims. Crucially, the Court held that Canafric's systematic post-test failure analyses separated its experimental methodology from mere "trial and error," that failed recipe formulations that allowed Canafric to eliminate specific hypotheses constituted a valid technological advancement, and that the Respondent had failed to address the Appellant's evidence in a forthright manner, especially the documentation provided to the CRA and the detailed technical discussions at the on-site meetings, other than by denying the claim. The decision in Canafric has already shaped subsequent Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, being cited in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King, 2024 TCC 159 (at para. 16), and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, 2025 TCC 63 (Dockets 2019-894(IT)G and 2021-1471(IT)G), and being referenced in commentary on BlackBerry Limited v. The King, 2023 TCC 137 (an expert-evidence ruling in a foreign accrual property income dispute, not an SR&ED case).
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous examination of Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108)—situated within the broader body of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence cited by the Court—exposes two intersecting layers of legal and evidentiary failure. First, it reveals the exact technical, documentary, and commercial flashpoints in Canafric's initial filings and audit interactions that provoked the CRA to disallow seven projects across four consecutive years. Second, it highlights the evidentiary and substantive shortcomings that frequently cause SR&ED litigants to lose at the Tax Court of Canada—as illustrated by the 2023 SR&ED Stakeholders webcast (November 30, 2023), which reviewed eight SR&ED cases resolved in 2022–2023 (two wins, Buhler Versatile and Canafric, and six losses) and noted that the six unsuccessful appellants were unable to prove they had identified a technological uncertainty and sought to resolve it through experimentation or analysis; those losses were Gestion ACBK Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC), Anne-Marie Chagnon Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (2022 TCC), JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC), Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 127, and 9158-1629 Quebec Inc. v. The King (2022 TCC)—contrasted against the tactical litigation failures committed by the Crown in defending the Minister's reassessments against Canafric.
Commercial Retail Specifications Versus Objective Technological Uncertainty

As the Court found, a major source of disagreement for all of the SR&ED claims was the CRA advisor's position that each breakthrough was transferable from one product to another—for example, that salt- and fat-reduction techniques could be replicated across different products. Because Canafric developed frozen pies for customers (such as Costco, Loblaw's, Metro, Mortimer's and Longo's) that specified targets for content, shelf life, taste acceptability and texture, the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), David Zhou—whose prior industry experience was mainly with high-sugar confectionery products and who had joined the CRA in early 2015—treated the challenges as repetitive across products; the Court described him as a generalist whose approach lacked the understanding necessary to properly evaluate the operations in question.

In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, the boundary between commercial product customization and true technological uncertainty is strictly policed. As Chief Justice Rossiter stated in Canafric (at para. 89), citing Justice D'Auray in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 42 (at para. 93), technological uncertainty is assessed on an objective, field-wide standard: "the lacking knowledge must really not exist in the base of scientific or technological knowledge, not simply be unknown to the claimant." Similarly, in Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 127, the Court dismissed an injection moulding manufacturer's appeal because resolving defects in custom client prototypes relied on standard CNC machining and moulding procedures rather than overcoming an objective knowledge gap in materials or mechanical engineering. Furthermore, as the CRA clarified when it removed the term "routine engineering" from its SR&ED Glossary on April 24, 2015, engineering or food science practice is never eligible on its own; rather, technical professionals only perform eligible SR&ED when their work constitutes experimental development aimed at overcoming a scientific or technological uncertainty under paragraph 248(1)(c) or directly supports such experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(d).

The Reasons in Canafric do not attribute the administrative dispute to the wording of Canafric's Form T661 narratives; rather, the dispute stemmed from the RTA's view that balancing "health" and "taste" demands posed the same, transferable challenge from one product to the next, combined with his view that the supporting documentation was insufficient. When a claimant describes a project on Form T661 as developing a healthier or better-tasting frozen pie to meet a grocery retailer's product brief, CRA auditors routinely classify the work as ineligible market-driven recipe formulation or routine quality control. At trial, Canafric overcame this hurdle because Mr. Pandya clearly demonstrated that the challenges were not transferable, since ingredients react differently when used in different products—a result conceptually similar to, though not expressly based on, the system uncertainty recognized in Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18, which Canafric does not cite. Mr. Pandya described project-specific challenges—including reducing salt and fat while preserving taste, achieving shelf-life targets without artificial preservatives, maintaining product integrity through the freeze/thaw process, increasing protein levels by 35%, replacing potato flakes with real potatoes and using leaner beef, using antibiotic-free meat with reduced cooking times, developing a thicker filling and a flaky crust compatible with all fillings (where the filling leaked moisture into the pastry), meeting halal requirements, and making lard-free pastry with at least 10% real butter—and the Court accepted that, because each project involved a new or improved product, there was no information available on how to achieve these goals.
The "Trial and Error" Characterization and Lack of Explicit Analytical Bridges

The second major point of contention centred on the second and third Northwest Hydraulic criteria: whether Canafric formulated specific hypotheses and tested them in accordance with the total discipline of the scientific method. The CRA's position was that Canafric relied on a "trial and error" approach—trying various recipes to reach its targets without attempting to explain or analyze the reason why each recipe did not work.

The Tax Court has consistently held that trial and error, if used alone, does not come within the scientific method, so a finding that testing was conducted by trial and error alone is generally fatal to the third criterion. In Flavor Net Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 179 (at paras. 53–55), cited in Canafric, the Court found that the testing was by and large done by trial and error and that the third requirement was not met; Béton Mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 278 (at para. 50), also cited in Canafric, is to the same effect; and in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, the appellant's own evidence described a process of "trial and error"—in each case, the claimant failed to demonstrate a structured causal link between one failed test and the design of the next. Where a claimant tests Option A, observes that it fails, and immediately moves to Option B without performing a diagnostic root-cause analysis of why Option A failed, the methodology is legally classified as routine trial and error rather than a "systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis" under subsection 248(1).

In Canafric, the CRA's position was precisely that Canafric had tried various recipes without attempting to explain or analyze why each recipe did not work. At trial, Chief Justice Rossiter rejected the CRA's "trial and error" characterization based on a pivotal evidentiary finding: when a recipe could not meet client requirements, Canafric's main takeaway was not simply that it did not work; Canafric "conducted analyses in order to understand which requirement was not met" and modified specific parts of the recipe in order to address the issue, while being limited by its clients' demands regarding which ingredients to use. This explicit analytical bridge—identifying which requirement was not met after an unsuccessful recipe before modifying specific parts of it—was sufficient, on the evidence, for the Court to find satisfied the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic.
Misconception of Failed Formulations and Technological Advancement

A third legal conflict arose under the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion regarding whether Canafric's projects resulted in a "technological advancement". Canafric was unable to achieve all of its targets: for example, project 1306 could not reach the 10-day shelf life (external laboratory testing showed the product became unsafe for human consumption after six days), and project 1501 was not successful because the product was not firm enough to be hand-held and did not achieve the required shelf life. On this criterion, the RTA testified that for project 1304 he did not have enough documentation to conclude there was a technological advancement, and for project 1501 he considered that only the first of the twelve products posed a technological uncertainty because the knowledge gained was transferable to the others.

Canadian jurisprudence establishes two strict boundaries regarding technological advancement. On one hand, product novelty or commercial success is legally insufficient on its own to prove technological advancement; as held in R&D PRO-innovation Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 186 (at para. 38), "[n]ovelty or innovation in a product is not sufficient to illustrate technological advancement." Similarly, in Highweb & Page Group Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 137, inflated business language claiming that a project "created unlimited scalability" was dismissed by the Tax Court as a mere "statement of business fact" rather than an advancement in underlying technological knowledge, whereas a specific sub-claim identifying a concrete technical incompatibility between .NET and Java that could not be resolved with accessible standard products was allowed.

On the other hand, CRA auditors frequently err by equating technical or commercial failure with the absence of technological advancement. Chief Justice Rossiter reaffirmed in Canafric that achieving technological advancement under paragraph 248(1)(c) requires the generation or discovery of knowledge that advances the understanding of science or technology recognizable to experts in the field, which expressly includes the rejection of a hypothesis. Although Canafric was unable to achieve all of its targets, the Tax Court held that the elimination of certain recipes which did not work constituted a technological advancement satisfying Criterion 4.
Contemporaneous Documentation Deficiencies Versus Oral Testimony and Ex Post Facto Reconstructions

The most contentious evidentiary dispute in Canafric revolved around the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion: whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed. During the September 14, 2015 on-site meeting (for the 2013 taxation year) and the March 8, 2018 on-site meeting (convened for projects 1501 and 1502 in the 2015 and 2016 taxation years, with the RTA focusing on project 1501), Mr. Pandya conveyed substantial technical information orally to the CRA reviewers, later supporting those discussions with documentary records. The RTA acknowledged a technological uncertainty in projects 1304 and 1306 but found the supporting documentation insufficient, CRA witnesses maintained that oral or anecdotal evidence is not sufficient in itself, and the 2014 claim was rejected under section 5.11.0 of the CRA's Claim Review Manual after the scheduled conference call did not take place.

At paragraph 86 of Canafric—in confirming the continued authority of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria rather than in addressing the documentation requirement—Chief Justice Rossiter cited the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (at para. 12), which affirmed National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47; on the documentation requirement itself, the Court relied on RIS-Christie, Formadrain, Béton Mobile and Flavor Net (at paras. 105–110). The contrast between National R&D and Canafric illustrates the most dangerous evidentiary trap in Canadian SR&ED litigation. In National R&D, the taxpayer succeeded in proving technological uncertainty under Criterion 1, but lost the appeal because the Court found that Criteria 2 through 5 were not met; on Criterion 5, the claimant admitted under cross-examination that its 50-experiment summary table was "created after the fact for the CRA" (2020 TCC 47, para. 71), and his testimony did not make up for the inadequate documentation (para. 73). When contingency consultants or claimants reconstruct technical narratives and experiment tables second-hand from memory at year-end or during an audit, the Tax Court is unlikely to accept such retroactive reconstructions as contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained (2020 TCC 47, paras. 71–72).

Conversely, the Reasons in Canafric contain no finding that Canafric's records were reconstructed after the fact. Rather, Canafric provided both documentary evidence (including T4 slips, payroll records, timesheets, letters and invoices, a 120-page document describing the product development work, and a project summary, recipe examples and a product sensory evaluation form for project 1501) and testimonial evidence, and Chief Justice Rossiter reiterated, relying on RIS-Christie, Formadrain and Béton Mobile, that documentary evidence is not mandatory and that testimonial evidence may be presented in support of a claim, while noting that not adequately documenting an SR&ED project is a riskier approach for claimants. Nevertheless, from an advisory perspective, relying on trial testimony to cure sparse contemporaneous documentation is an expensive, high-risk posture: Canafric's dispute ran from the first reassessment dated May 13, 2016 (for the 2013 taxation year) to the July 26, 2023 judgment. Embedding diagnostic failure analyses directly into dated, immutable batch logs as the work progresses remains essential to neutralize Criterion 5 objections during the initial CRA review.
Contractual and Commercial Production Overlaps in Retailer-Driven Development

While the dispute in Canafric centred on whether the projects constituted eligible SR&ED under subsection 248(1), Canafric's commercial model—developing custom frozen pies to meet the demands of large grocery retailers such as Costco, Loblaws, and Mortimer—exposes claimants to severe contractual and statutory exclusion risks under the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 127(9) and section 37, a taxpayer's qualified SR&ED expenditures must be reduced by any "contract payment," which includes any amount payable by a taxable Canadian corporation (such as Loblaws or Costco Canada) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. Where a manufacturer enters into custom formulation or private-label supply agreements with Canadian retailers that commingle product development fees, slotting allowances, or guaranteed purchase commitments with R&D milestones, CRA Financial Reviewers routinely assert that the manufacturer is performing contract research on the retailer's behalf, stripping the claimant of its ITCs. To prevent disqualification, commercial contracts must clearly establish a contract for the sale of commercial goods rather than a contract for R&D services, allocating 100% of the financial R&D risk and foreground technical intellectual property (formulations, process parameters, and manufacturing know-how) to the manufacturer.

Simultaneously, scaling up food formulations for commercial retail clients implicates paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (i) of the Act, which exclude quality control or routine testing and commercial production (issues the Court did not need to address in Canafric, where Mr. Pandya explained that plant trials only proceeded once a product met all customer requirements). When experimental batches transition from a test kitchen to industrial production lines, failing to maintain strict accounting and operational boundaries between experimental scale-up runs (aimed at resolving shear, thermal, or moisture uncertainties) and commercial pre-production runs (aimed at generating retail buyer samples or commercial inventory) triggers broad expenditure disallowances.
The Crown's Evidentiary and Procedural Failure at Trial

Finally, Canafric exposes a decisive procedural failure by the Respondent (the Crown) in SR&ED tax litigation. In Tax Court of Canada proceedings, once the Appellant adduces credible, reliable technical evidence establishing a prima facie case that demolishes the Minister's assumptions across the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—as Canafric accomplished through Mr. Pandya's comprehensive testimony and supporting documentation—the tactical burden shifts to the Crown to rebut that evidence. Chief Justice Rossiter found that the Respondent failed to address the Appellant's evidence in a forthright manner, especially the documentation provided to the CRA and the detailed technical discussions which took place during the on-site meetings, observing pointedly: "This was never addressed by the Respondent other than by denying the claim." Although the Respondent called three CRA witnesses (George Papadopoulos, Azza Hassanein and David Zhou), the Court found Mr. Zhou to be a generalist whose approach lacked the understanding necessary to properly evaluate the operations in question, no independent expert evidence in food science is mentioned in the Reasons, and the Court allowed the appeals for all four taxation years, inviting written submissions on costs.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial SR&ED requirement examined in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) against the specific administrative challenges raised by the CRA (alongside comparative taxpayer failures in Canadian TCC jurisprudence) and the governing standard of proof applied by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Statutory & Judicial Requirement (Income Tax Act & Northwest Hydraulic)
CRA Disallowance Rationale & Common Taxpayer Failure Modes
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Holding in Canafric (2023 TCC 108)

cells: 1. Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q1; Formadrain, 2017 TCC 42)

CRA Allegation: The RTA took the position that salt- and fat-reduction techniques were transferable from one product to another (and, for project 1602, that "a pie is a pie"), while acknowledging a technological uncertainty in projects 1304 and 1306 and in the first product of project 1501. Common Failure Mode: Framing objectives as commercial/market goals rather than objective knowledge gaps (Mold Leaders, 2023 TCC 127; Highweb, 2015 TCC 137).

Standard of Proof: Balance of probabilities demonstrating an objective insufficiency in the existing scientific/technological knowledge base—including system uncertainty where known components interact unpredictably under competing constraints (Buhler Versatile, 2023 TCC 18). Holding: Satisfied; based on the challenges described by Mr. Pandya (salt and fat reduction while preserving taste, shelf life without artificial preservatives, freeze/thaw integrity, and other project-specific requirements), projects 1304, 1306, 1401, 1402, 1501 and 1502 posed a technological uncertainty, because ingredients react differently in different products and the techniques were therefore not transferable.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q2; CW Agencies, 2001 FCA 393)

CRA Allegation: The Reasons record no distinct CRA objection under this criterion; the CRA's challenge to the "how" requirement centred on the alleged "trial and error" approach under the third criterion. Common Failure Mode: Stating commercial targets ("create a low-sodium pie") instead of causal variable relationships.

Standard of Proof: Proof that the claimant articulated specific, testable propositions correlating independent technical variables to predicted physical, chemical, or mechanical outcomes aimed at reducing the identified uncertainty. Holding: Satisfied; the Court held that Canafric's development process (client request, recipe elaboration, testing against requirements, and taste-panel evaluation) met the second criterion because Canafric formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at achieving its various goals.
3. Total Discipline of the Scientific Method (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q3; Hypercube, 2015 TCC 65)

CRA Allegation: Recipe development was conducted via unguided "trial and error"—discarding failed batches and trying new combinations until a recipe succeeded. Common Failure Mode: Using "trial and error" language in T661 narratives or failing to document analytical steps between failed tests (Zeuter, 2006 TCC 597).

Standard of Proof: Demonstration of a structured, iterative cycle of hypothesis formulation, controlled testing, quantitative/qualitative observation, and root-cause failure analysis driving subsequent modifications. Holding: Satisfied; Canafric "conducted analyses in order to understand which requirement was not met" when a recipe could not meet client requirements, and modified specific parts of the recipe to address the issue.
4. Technological Advancement (ITA s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Q4; R&D PRO-innovation, 2015 TCC 186)

CRA Allegation: For project 1304, the RTA found insufficient documentation to conclude there was a technological advancement; for project 1501, he considered that only the first of twelve products posed a technological uncertainty. Common Failure Mode: Conflating commercial product novelty with knowledge generation, or abandoning claims when experiments fail.

Standard of Proof: Generation or discovery of new technological knowledge recognizable to a person skilled in the art, which expressly includes incremental process/material improvements and the rejection of a hypothesis, even where the project's objectives were not met. Holding: Satisfied; the elimination of certain recipes which did not work constituted a technological advancement, even though Canafric was unable to achieve all of its targets.
5. Contemporaneous Record-Keeping (ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Q5; National R&D, 2022 FCA 72)

CRA Allegation: The RTA found the supporting documentation for projects 1304 and 1306 insufficient, and CRA witnesses testified that anecdotal or oral evidence is not sufficient in itself without independent objective evidence. Common Failure Mode: Fabricating or reconstructing experiment tables ex post facto for CRA auditors (National R&D, 2020 TCC 47, para. 71).

Standard of Proof: Contemporaneous records of hypotheses tested and results kept as work progressed are expected, but credible, reliable firsthand oral testimony may be presented in support of a claim, since documentary evidence is not mandatory (RIS-Christie; Formadrain; Béton Mobile), although inadequate documentation is a riskier approach. Holding: Satisfied; Canafric provided both documentary and testimonial evidence, Mr. Pandya's testimony was found credible and reliable, and the Respondent did not address that evidence other than by denying the claim.
6. Commercial Production & Contract Payment Exclusions (ITA ss. 37(1), 127(9), 248(1)(e)–(k))

CRA Audit Risk: Developing custom products for Canadian retailers (Costco, Loblaws) triggers challenges that work is either commercial production/quality control or funded via "contract payments". Common Failure Mode: Ambiguous supply contracts that commingle R&D service fees with product sales or fail to segregate commercial runs.

Standard of Proof: Taxpayer must demonstrate that expenditures were incurred for experimental development (not commercial production or routine quality control) and that client revenues were strictly for commercial goods sold, with IP and R&D risk retained by the claimant. Holding: Not addressed in Canafric, which turned solely on eligibility under subsection 248(1); the appeals were allowed in full, with the disallowed expenditures ($343,449+) and ITCs ($60,963+) reinstated across 2013–2016.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) into actionable compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic projects confronting the exact legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary vulnerabilities highlighted in the ruling. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome CRA audit objections and satisfy subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Commercial Food Manufacturing and Bioprocessing
Project Scenario and Audit Vulnerability Profile

Northern Hearth Foods Ltd. ("Northern Hearth") is an Ontario-based CCPC specializing in commercial frozen bakery and prepared meal manufacturing, filing under Guide T4088 Field of Science or Technology Codes 2.11.01 (Food and beverages) and 2.04.01 (Chemical engineering). A major Canadian grocery retail chain ("Retailer X") engages Northern Hearth to supply a new line of plant-based, gluten-free, low-sodium frozen savoury turnovers. Retailer X mandates that the product achieve a minimum 12-month frozen shelf life at −18°C, contain less than 140 mg of sodium per serving, utilize a clean-label hydrocolloid-free binding matrix, and withstand commercial high-speed automated encrusting and spiral blast-freezing without crust micro-fissuring or filling syneresis (water separation) upon consumer re-thermalization.

In its un-remediated state, Northern Hearth exhibits four fatal SR&ED vulnerabilities mirroring the audit disputes in Canafric and related TCC jurisprudence. First, the R&D team frames the project in internal memos and draft Form T661 narratives around commercial retail objectives—describing the goal as developing a gluten-free, low-sodium plant-based turnover to satisfy Retailer X's clean-label market specifications and sensory taste panels—which invites immediate disallowance under Formadrain (2017 TCC 42) and Highweb (2015 TCC 137) as routine culinary adaptation and market research. Second, over an eight-month period, food technologists run 42 kitchen and pilot-line batches varying pea protein isolate, modified tapioca starch, and lipid ratios, recording only ingredient weights and pass/fail sensory remarks (such as "Batch 14: Crust cracked during freezing; too dry; rejected") without documenting any diagnostic analysis between batches, exposing the claim to fatal "trial and error" disqualification under Hypercube (2015 TCC 65) and Zeuter (2006 TCC 597). Third, Northern Hearth signs a vendor onboarding agreement with Retailer X that includes a $50,000 "Product Development & Slotting Allowance" credit and states that the custom turnover recipe is "developed exclusively for Retailer X," triggering a subsection 127(9) "contract payment" reduction by CRA Financial Reviewers. Fourth, at year-end, an external contingency consultant interviews the lead food scientist from memory and constructs a retroactive 42-row experiment summary table for the CRA audit, replicating the after-the-fact documentation failure penalized in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 47, para. 71; aff'd 2022 FCA 72).
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance

Northern Hearth must establish a formal SR&ED Technical Governance Charter prior to commencing formulation trials, enforcing a strict institutional separation between commercial retail objectives and objective scientific or technological uncertainties. Before project initiation, the Lead Food Scientist must execute and archive a dated Knowledge Base Baseline Assessment documenting why standard food science formulations and published ingredient supplier guidelines cannot resolve the competing physical and chemical constraints. Specifically, the baseline governance document must record that while gluten-free dough hydration and low-sodium emulsions are individually established in standard food processing, eliminating synthetic hydrocolloids (such as xanthan gum or methylcellulose) while simultaneously reducing sodium below 140 mg per serving removes the ionic protein-solubilizing capacity required to stabilize the pea-protein emulsion. This system interaction induces rapid amylopectin retrogradation and free-water migration across the starch-lipid barrier during spiral blast-freezing, constituting an objective technological (system) uncertainty within the meaning of Northwest Hydraulic, consistent with the approach applied in Canafric.

Concurrently, project governance must implement strict stage-gate accounting cost centres to segregate eligible experimental development under paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d) from excluded activities under paragraphs 248(1)(e), (f) and (i). Gate 0 (Cost Centre 100-COM) must capture and exclude all marketing meetings with Retailer X, culinary ideation, focus group taste panels, and nutritional label costing. Gate 1 (Cost Centre 200-SRED) is activated strictly for bench-scale rheological testing, water-activity (a<sub>w</sub>) modelling, differential scanning calorimetry, and pilot-line shear-stress trials aimed at resolving the protein-lipid-starch phase separation and crust micro-fissuring. Once the formulation parameters and thermal processing curves are established, Gate 2 (Cost Centre 300-PROD) immediately closes the SR&ED cost collector, routing all subsequent microbiological shelf-life verification, nutritional assay certification, and commercial packaging runs to regular production overhead.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation

To satisfy Chief Justice Rossiter's decisive standard in Canafric (2023 TCC 108)—that the taxpayer "conducted analyses in order to understand which requirement was not met"—Northern Hearth must replace subjective pass/fail recipe cards with a mandatory, four-part Formulation Experimentation and Root-Cause Diagnostic Protocol inside its electronic laboratory notebook (ELN). Technical narratives and batch logs must eliminate subjective culinary terminology ("taste," "mouthfeel," "too dry") and record all observations using objective physico-chemical metrics, including water activity (aw), dynamic viscosity (η, in mPa·s, at specified shear rates), moisture migration percentage across the crust-filling interface, glass transition temperature (Tg), and tensile fracture force (Fmax, in N) via texture profile analysis (TPA).

Within the ELN workflow, the software architecture must programmatically lock the creation of Batch N+1 until the Lead Food Scientist completes the diagnostic failure analysis for Batch N. For example, in Batch 14, the scientist first logs the explicit hypothesis (H14): that increasing pre-gelatinized waxy maize starch from 3.5% to 5.0% w/w while pre-emulsifying sunflower oil with citrus fibre at 1.5% w/w will bind free water within the plant-protein matrix, maintaining filling viscosity above 8,000 mPa·s and keeping crust moisture uptake below 2.0% after 14 days of accelerated freeze-thaw cycling. Second, the scientist logs the controlled experimental execution parameters, including exact mixing shear speeds (rpm), hydration temperatures, and blast-freezer thermal profiles. Third, the scientist records the quantitative test results, noting that filling viscosity dropped to 3,200 mPa·s upon thawing, crust moisture uptake reached 6.8%, and micro-fissures developed along the dorsal seam. Fourth—forming the crucial Canafric analytical bridge—the scientist documents the root-cause failure analysis: microscopic and moisture-balance evaluation revealed that high-shear automated encrusting at 2,800 rpm mechanically ruptured the citrus-fibre lipid droplets, releasing unbound water during ice-crystal nucleation at −12°C. This documented analysis rejects hypothesis H14, establishes the technological advancement that mechanical shear degradation rather than thermal gelatinization insufficiency drives the syneresis, and directly governs the formulation of hypothesis H15 (testing low-shear cold-hydration protein cross-linking via transglutaminase).
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms

Northern Hearth's tax and commercial counsel must restructure its Master Supply and Private-Label Manufacturing Agreement with Retailer X to eliminate any statutory risk that client payments constitute "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) of the Act. The contract must include an explicit characterization clause stipulating that the agreement is exclusively a commercial contract for the manufacture and sale of finished food products on a per-case wholesale basis, and that under no circumstances is Retailer X engaging, funding, or remunerating Northern Hearth to perform scientific research or experimental development on Retailer X's behalf.

Furthermore, the $50,000 onboarding credit must be removed from any "Product Development" nomenclature and structured strictly as a commercial volume rebate tied to retail shelf placement and case-volume purchasing commitments, accompanied by an explicit representation that Northern Hearth bears 100% of the financial risk of all internal product formulation, process engineering, and failed experimental trials. With respect to intellectual property, while Retailer X retains ownership of its consumer-facing trademark and packaging trade dress, the contract must vest 100% of the foreground technical IP—defined as all food science formulations, ingredient ratios, rheological processing parameters, thermal profiles, manufacturing know-how, and experimental data—exclusively in Northern Hearth. Granting Retailer X a time-limited commercial exclusivity period over the finished retail SKU remains commercially viable without jeopardizing SR&ED eligibility, provided the underlying technical know-how and process IP remain the exclusive property of Northern Hearth.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking

To insulate Northern Hearth against both the CRA's Criterion 5 documentation challenge in Canafric and the fatal retroactive reconstruction trap in National R&D (2020 TCC 47 / 2022 FCA 72), the company must deploy an immutable contemporaneous evidence trail. Every batch formulation sheet, texture analyzer trace, moisture balance readout, and post-batch failure analysis memo must be committed to an append-only digital repository with system-generated timestamps at the exact time each batch is evaluated, preserving verifiable provenance (repository, document hash, and timestamp). All failed formulations (such as Batches 1 through 38 that failed structural or syneresis thresholds) must be retained in the permanent SR&ED project dossier alongside their diagnostic failure analyses, providing contemporaneous proof of hypothesis rejection and knowledge generation under Criterion 4. Finally, time-tracking logs for the Lead Food Scientist and pilot-line technicians must be recorded weekly against specific experimental batch identifiers (SRED-PROJ1-B01 through B42), while raw ingredients consumed and scrapped during failed pilot runs are requisitioned under dedicated experimental ERP codes to substantiate deductible section 37 expenditures and prepare the Lead Food Scientist to deliver credible, firsthand testimony if required.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial Manufacturing and Polymer Material Engineering
Project Scenario and Audit Vulnerability Profile

Precision Thermo-Composites Inc. ("PTC") is an Alberta-based CCPC specializing in precision injection moulding, computer numerical control (CNC) tooling, and high-performance polymer composite components for the energy and heavy agricultural equipment sectors, filing under Guide T4088 Field of Science or Technology Codes 2.05.04 (Plastics, Rubber, and Composites) and 2.03.09 (Tooling, machinery, and equipment engineering and manufacturing). PTC undertakes an internal development project to engineer an ultra-lightweight, short-glass-fibre-reinforced polyetheretherketone (PEEK) hydraulic manifold valve body capable of withstanding continuous operating pressures of 35 MPa and cyclic thermal shocks from −40°C to 120°C without anisotropic warpage or micro-delamination at the intersecting internal fluid ports.

In its un-remediated state, PTC faces the exact legal pitfalls that resulted in the taxpayer's loss in Mold Leaders Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 127, alongside the evidentiary issues examined in Canafric (2023 TCC 108). First, PTC's engineers describe the project in internal shop orders and draft T661 narratives as "optimizing CNC mould gating and injection moulding cycle times to eliminate warpage in a custom PEEK valve manifold," which CRA RTAs will disallow as routine engineering and standard machine setup under Mold Leaders. Second, across 18 injection moulding press runs, engineers adjust melt temperature, pack pressure, and cooling duration without documenting why standard finite-element flow simulations (Moldflow) and resin supplier processing guides failed to predict the internal port delamination, presenting the appearance of unguided trial and error. Third, PTC utilizes the same multi-cavity production mould to run both experimental shear-stress trials and 500 commercial pre-production manifolds billed to an agricultural equipment original equipment manufacturer ("OEM Client Y"), commingling eligible experimental development with ineligible commercial production and funded tooling. Fourth, the Lead Polymer Engineer records informal, undated observations in a personal notebook while the T661 narrative relies on inflated claims of "breakthrough manifold durability" (Highweb, 2015 TCC 137), creating a severe disconnect between the documentary record and potential oral testimony.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance

To avoid the routine engineering disqualification suffered in Mold Leaders (2023 TCC 127) and align with the winning system-uncertainty frameworks in Canafric (2023 TCC 108) and Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 18, PTC must anchor its project governance in objective materials and system engineering uncertainty. Prior to cutting steel or scheduling press trials, the Vice President of Engineering must sign a formal Technological Uncertainty Definition Charter establishing why standard injection moulding practices and commercial finite-element flow software cannot resolve the manifold's structural failure. The charter must document that at 30% short-glass-fibre loading in a semi-crystalline PEEK matrix, high-velocity melt flow through intersecting internal hydraulic ports generates turbulent fountain-flow shear gradients that induce localized fibre-matrix de-bonding and orthotropic thermal contraction—a complex multi-variable regime where existing constitutive rheological equations fail to predict weld-line micro-delamination under −40°C to 120°C thermal shock cycling.

Project governance must also enforce a strict boundary between routine engineering and eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the Act. Standard CAD design of the external mounting flanges, routine CNC machining of the master mould base, and standard quality control coordinate-measuring machine (CMM) inspections must be routed to regular commercial tooling job codes and excluded from the SR&ED claim. Conversely, designing and machining modular, sacrificial shear-modifying core pins and variable-geometry rheological test inserts specifically required to test hypotheses regarding glass-fibre orientation tensors and crystalline morphology are authorized under a dedicated SR&ED Engineering Change Request (ECR-SRED-2026) as engineering and tooling work "directly in support of and commensurate with the needs" of the paragraph 248(1)(c) experimental development.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation

In industrial moulding and machining, CRA RTAs frequently disallow claims because adjusting machine controller settings (melt temperature, injection velocity, holding pressure) appears indistinguishable from routine machine setup or trial and error. To satisfy the third and fourth Northwest Hydraulic criteria under the Canafric template, PTC must prohibit unexplained parameter tables and mandate a Scientific Method Experimentation Log that documents a rigorous root-cause diagnostic analysis after every press run.

For each experimental press run (Run 1 through Run 18), the Lead Polymer Engineer must document four sequential analytical elements. First, the engineer states the specific hypothesis (H4): that introducing a counter-rotating annular flow restrictor at Port B while maintaining mould wall temperature at 200°C (above the PEEK glass transition threshold of 143°C) will align glass fibres tangentially across the knit-line interface, achieving a uniform degree of crystallinity between 30% and 35% and preventing micro-delamination at 105 MPa burst pressure. Second, the engineer records the controlled testing protocols, utilizing destructive cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray micro-tomography (micro-CT) for 3D fibre-orientation tensor mapping, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) for percent crystallinity, and hydraulic impulse fatigue testing. Third, the engineer logs the empirical failure data: Run 4 specimens suffered inter-laminar fracture at 62 MPa after 1,200 thermal cycles. Fourth, executing the Canafric analytical bridge, the engineer records the diagnostic failure analysis: cross-sectional SEM and DSC assays demonstrated that while the annular restrictor aligned fibres along the outer skin, the narrow throat induced excessive shear heating (+28°C above nominal melt temperature) in the core layer, retarding core crystallization (22% core crystallinity versus 34% skin crystallinity) and generating severe internal residual stress gradients. This analysis explains precisely why the requirement was not met, proves a technological advancement through the rejection of H4, and directly dictates the design of Run 5 (testing a stepped-compression core pin geometry paired with conformal pulsed-cooling channels). All T661 narratives are then generated directly from these technical logs, eliminating business hyperbole (Highweb, 2015 TCC 137) and self-defeating "trial and error" phrasing (Hypercube, 2015 TCC 65).
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms

To prevent OEM Client Y's commercial payments from disqualifying PTC's expenditures as "contract payments" under subsection 127(9) or tainting the experimental runs as commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i), PTC's legal counsel must restructure the commercial supply arrangements prior to project execution. PTC must avoid entering into a "Custom Prototype & R&D Service Contract" billed on engineering milestones. Instead, PTC must execute a standard Commercial Component Supply Agreement governing the future sale of production-certified manifolds at a fixed per-unit price once commercial manufacturing commences.

With respect to tooling revenues, if OEM Client Y pays a tooling charge, the contract must explicitly restrict that payment to the fabrication of the commercial multi-cavity production mould base constructed after experimental development is concluded. All modular experimental test inserts, sacrificial core pins, and destructively tested PEEK specimens fabricated during the SR&ED phase must be funded by PTC from its internal R&D budget without customer reimbursement. Furthermore, the contract must bifurcate intellectual property ownership: while OEM Client Y retains ownership of the external dimensional envelope and mounting interface specifications of the valve body, PTC retains exclusive title to all foreground Polymer Processing and Rheological Tooling IP, encompassing all gating geometries, shear-control insert designs, and thermal crystallization profiles generated during the experimental program.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and reinforce oral witness credibility under the principles of Canafric (2023 TCC 108) and National R&D (2022 FCA 72), PTC must synchronize its shop-floor ERP system, CAD/FEA repositories, and witness preparation protocols. Every modification to the experimental mould insert geometry in CAD and every finite-element simulation file must be committed to a local, version-controlled repository with an immutable timestamp and commit log linking the geometry change to the prior run's diagnostic failure report. On the shop floor, experimental press trials must be scheduled under a dedicated ERP work-order series (WO-SRED-EXP) strictly segregated from commercial production runs (WO-PROD), with machine controller data traces (cavity pressure transducers, thermocouple logs, and cycle timestamps) archived automatically on the date of testing. Finally, following the example of Mr. Pandya in Canafric, PTC must designate its Lead Polymer Engineer—who personally directed the press trials and SEM/DSC failure analyses across every phase of the project—to attend all CRA on-site review meetings and serve as the primary witness of record, ensuring that any minor gaps in the shop-floor logs are seamlessly bridged by authoritative, firsthand technical testimony.
Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 108) establishes three foundational legal and compliance imperatives for Canadian SR&ED claimants and tax advisors. First, SR&ED eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is fundamentally sector-neutral: traditional industries such as commercial food processing and industrial manufacturing are fully entitled to section 37 deductions and section 127 ITCs whenever competing physical, chemical, or mechanical parameters create objective system uncertainties that cannot be resolved through standard procedures. Second, the legal dividing line between an eligible "systematic investigation or search" and fatal "trial and error" rests on the documented analytical bridge between iterations—specifically, proving that after each failed test, the taxpayer "conducted analyses in order to understand which requirement was not met" before modifying the hypothesis for the subsequent test, and recognizing that failed experiments that eliminate unviable hypotheses constitute genuine technological advancement. Third, while claimants must never fabricate or retroactively reconstruct experiment tables for an audit (National R&D, 2020 TCC 47 / 2022 FCA 72), Canafric confirms that documentary evidence is not mandatory and that documentary records combined with credible, reliable testimony from a senior witness involved at every stage of the CRA review process (in Canafric, the CEO, who oversaw the development work) can satisfy the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion, leaving the Crown to answer that evidence.

outcome: Appeal allowed; court held systematic, documented experimentation resolving unpredictable variable interactions qualified as SR&ED.
